source_text: Verum ne tu detectum temet inspiciens, illo tentes erumpere, ut referas non te dixisse: Ideo malum ortum est in opere Dei, quoniam ex nihilo factum est; sed: Ideo potuit oboriri, quia ex nihilo factum est; ostendendum est, quanto violentioribus laqueis illigeris. Si enim dixeris possibilitatem te mali, non necessitatem, aeterni illius nihili viribus imputasse; nos referimus, quod potuit oriri mala voluntas in homine, non est certe aliud quam arbitrium liberum; ideo enim potuit oriri mala voluntas, ut oriri posset et bona. Haec libertas est, in qua se ratio exercet, propter quod ad imaginem Dei homo factus asseritur, per quam creaturis ceteris antecellit. Si ergo quod in homine mala voluntas potuit exoriri, nihil est aliud quam arbitrii libertas; et hoc tantum est, ut per eius insignia ceteris antistet animantibus; tu qui hanc possibilitatem profiteris ideo fuisse in homine, non quia a Deo, sed quia de nihilo factus est, novo dogmatis prodigio illud nihil, id est, antiquam inanitatem, tanti boni, id est, liberi arbitrii causam pronuntias. Denique ut res brevi interrogatione lucescat; hoc quod dixisti: Nec ideo tamen potuit oriri voluntas mala, quia a Deo factus est homo, sed ideo quia de nihilo factus est homo; hoc, inquam, ipsum quod potuit oriri voluntas, bonum esse, an malum credis? Id est, ipsam facultatem oriendae voluntatis, quam nihilo reputavisti, probam arbitraris, an pessimam? Si bonam dixeris: ergo non Deus est boni causa, sed nihilum. Sin autem, hoc esse insanissimum videns, malam eam pronuntiaveris; quippe quam dicis non Deo reputandam esse, sed nihilo; protestaberis nos nihil adversum te collegisse versute, sed bona disputandi fide malam fidem tui dogmatis subruisse. Stat ergo inconcussum quod egimus, te videlicet et Manichaeum, etiam primi hominis voluntatem malam necessitati aeternae originis imputasse.
pass_a_gloss: But lest you, inspecting yourself detected, try to burst out there, that you report you did not say: Therefore evil arose in a work of God, because it was made from nothing; but: Therefore it could arise, because it was made from nothing; it must be shown by how much more violent nooses you are bound. For if you shall have said that you credited a possibility of evil, not a necessity, to the powers of that eternal nothing; we report that what an evil will could arise in a human is certainly nothing other than free decision; for therefore an evil will could arise, that a good also could arise. This is the freedom in which reason exercises itself, on account of which the human is asserted made to the image of God, through which he stands before the rest of creatures. If therefore that an evil will could arise in a human is nothing other than freedom of decision; and this is so much, that through its insignia he stands before other living beings; you who profess that this possibility was in the human therefore, not because by God, but because he was made from nothing, by a new portent of dogma pronounce that nothing, that is the ancient emptiness, the cause of so great a good, that is of free decision. Finally that the matter may shine by a brief interrogation; this which you said: Nor nevertheless therefore could an evil will arise, because the human was made by God, but therefore because the human was made from nothing; this itself, I say, that a will could arise, do you believe to be good, or evil? That is, the faculty itself of a will about to arise, which you credited to nothing, do you judge proven, or worst? If you shall have said good: therefore God is not the cause of good, but nothing. But if, seeing this to be most insane, you shall have pronounced it evil; seeing that you say it is not to be credited to God, but to nothing; you will protest that we gathered nothing against you cunningly, but by a good faith of disputing undermined the evil faith of your dogma. That therefore stands unshaken which we did, namely that you and Manichaeus credited even the first human's evil will to a necessity of eternal origin.

pass_b_english: But lest, seeing yourself exposed, you try to break out by replying that you did not say, ‘Evil arose in God’s work because it was made from nothing,’ but rather, ‘Evil could arise because it was made from nothing,’ we must show how much more tightly the snares bind you. If you say that you attributed evil’s possibility, not its necessity, to the powers of that eternal nothing, we reply: the fact that an evil will could arise in a human being is certainly nothing other than free will. An evil will could arise precisely so that a good will could arise too. This is the freedom in which reason exercises itself, on account of which the human being is declared made in God’s image, and by which he excels other creatures (Genesis 1:26–27). If, then, the possibility of an evil will’s arising in a human being is nothing other than freedom of will, and this is so great a thing that its distinction makes him surpass the other living creatures, you who profess that this possibility existed in him not because he was made by God but because he was made from nothing declare, by a new monstrosity of doctrine, that nothing—ancient emptiness—is the cause of so great a good as free will.

To make the matter clear with a brief question: you said, ‘The evil will could arise not because the human being was made by God, but because he was made from nothing.’ This very possibility of the will’s arising, I ask, do you believe it good or evil? That is, do you judge the capacity for a will to arise, which you attributed to nothing, good or utterly evil? If you call it good, then God is not the cause of the good: nothing is. But if, seeing this to be completely insane, you declare it evil—since you say it should be attributed not to God but to nothing—you will testify that we reached no deceitful conclusion against you, but with honest debate overthrew your doctrine’s evil faith. Our result therefore stands unshaken: you and Mani have attributed even the first man’s evil will to the necessity of an eternal origin.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
